_meta.purpose: Real published figures for SLATE journeys: premium airline cabins, jet lag physiology, and a car as a journey leg (US, UK, Ireland).
_meta.rules: Every figure carries source_url and the date or period it applies to. 'verification' says how the figure was read: 'fetched' = read from the primary page or file itself; 'operator_excerpt' = the operator's own page returned 403 to the fetcher and the figure was read from a search-index excerpt of that same page; 'secondary' = a clearly labelled non-primary source. 'derived' fields are arithmetic on published figures and are marked as such; they are not published numbers. Anything not confirmable is null and explained in 'uncertain'.
_meta.currency_notes: US figures in USD, UK in GBP (pence for fuel), Ireland in EUR.

dot_consumer_airfare_report_scope.finding: The DOT Domestic Airline Fares Consumer Report's average fares are NOT economy-only. They are averages over all fare-paying passengers and include first-class fares; frequent-flyer award tickets are excluded.
dot_consumer_airfare_report_scope.quote: cover first class fares paid to carriers offering such service but does not cover free tickets, such as those awarded by carriers offering frequent flyer programs
dot_consumer_airfare_report_scope.period: Standing methodology wording in DOT Domestic Airline Fares Consumer Reports (seen in the 2024 Q1 edition)
dot_consumer_airfare_report_scope.verification: operator_excerpt (DOT PDF returned 403; wording read from the search-index excerpt of the DOT PDF)
dot_consumer_airfare_report_scope.implication_for_game: If SLATE treats the DOT average as the economy fare, it is slightly overstated for economy, because premium fares are blended in. The size of that bias is not published.

db1b_fare_class_codes.note: There is no premium-economy code in DB1B. 'W' is not a DB1B fare class code; premium economy is filed under whatever class the carrier reports, usually coach.
db1b_fare_class_codes.caveat: The GMU DB1B primer reports that DOT warns FareClass is coded inconsistently by carriers and should not be relied on for analysis.
db1b_fare_class_codes.verification: secondary (data-vendor and university documentation of the BTS field definitions; the BTS field page itself was not fetched)

average_fare_by_cabin_us.note: No BTS table or peer-reviewed analysis that publishes average fare or fare per mile by DB1B fare class was found. See 'uncertain'.

global_premium_to_economy_fare_ratio.unit: premium (first and business) average fare as a multiple of economy average fare
global_premium_to_economy_fare_ratio.quote: Premium fares, which are approximately five times higher than economy fares on average
global_premium_to_economy_fare_ratio.chart_range_note: The report's chart plots the first-and-business to economy fare ratio on an axis of 4.0 to 8.0, with seasonal swings (premium relatively dearer in Q2 and Q4).
global_premium_to_economy_fare_ratio.period: IATA Chart of the Week, 26 July 2024 (data Jan 2023 to May 2024)

premium_share_of_all_passengers_global.quote: Business and first-class (premium) passengers constitute a mere 3% of all travelers

premium_share_of_passenger_revenue_globa.quote: contribute significantly - about 15% - to passenger revenue (excluding ancillary income)

international_premium_passengers_2025.period: Calendar 2025 (IATA World Air Transport Statistics, released 16 July 2026)

delta_2025.note: Revenue split only; Delta does not publish passenger counts or average fare by cabin, so no fare ratio can be derived.

academic.citation: Hugon-Duprat C, O'Connell JF. The rationale for implementing a premium economy class in the long haul markets - Evidence from the transatlantic market. Journal of Air Transport Management 47 (2015) 11-19. doi:10.1016/j.jairtraman.2015.03.005
academic.finding: On British Airways London Heathrow to New York JFK (747-400), a premium economy seat costs about 1.6 times as much as an economy seat to produce, and the paper reports premium economy as the most profitable cabin; it also reports a 2.3 figure for revenue (see 'uncertain' for what it is relative to).
academic.period: Published August 2015; route data from the paper's study period
academic.verification: secondary (RePEc abstract listing; full text paywalled)

academic.citation: Kuo C-W, Jou R-C. Willingness to pay for airlines' premium economy class: The perspective of passengers. Journal of Air Transport Management 59 (2017) 134-142. doi:10.1016/j.jairtraman.2016.12.005
academic.finding: Stated willingness to pay to upgrade from economy to premium economy, round trip.
academic.caution: This is survey willingness to pay (Taiwanese travellers), not a published fare difference.
academic.verification: secondary (RePEc abstract listing; full text paywalled)

united.effective: tickets purchased on or after 2026-04-03 (a $10 increase per bag)
united.verification: secondary (united.com timed out; figures from NerdWallet and CNBC reporting)

delta.rule: Complimentary checked baggage for Delta One, Delta Premium Select, and Delta First and Business Class passengers. Weight: Main, Comfort and Premium Select 50 lb per piece; Delta One and Delta First 70 lb per piece.
delta.free_bag_count_verification: secondary (Delta's own pages fetched confirm 'complimentary' and the weights but not the count; the count of 2 comes from third-party guides)
delta.basic_fare_exception: Delta's Basic versions of premium cabins (First Basic, Premium Select Basic, 'Basic Business' in Delta One) carry a reduced checked-bag allowance.

american.rule: Customers who purchase seats in premium cabins on domestic and international flights continue to receive complimentary bags.

united.rule: From spring 2026 United splits Polaris (business) and Premium Plus (premium economy) into Base, Standard and Flexible tiers on long-haul international, premium transcontinental and some Hawaii routes. Base: 1 checked bag, United Club (not Polaris lounge) access for Polaris, paid seat selection, nonrefundable and no changes. Standard: 2 checked bags, Polaris lounge access (Polaris only), seat selection, changes allowed, nonrefundable. Flexible: as Standard but refundable. Premium Plus does not automatically include lounge access.
united.period: Announced 9 April 2026; rollout from mid to late April 2026, expanding through 2026
united.verification: secondary (AFAR; United's own release timed out)

lounge_access.delta_one_lounge: Same-day departing or arriving Delta One ticketed passengers may use the Delta One Lounge. Basic Business customers lose Delta One Lounge and Sky Club access for travel on or after 19 January 2027; a Delta One Classic or Extra fare is required.
lounge_access.period: 2026, with the Basic Business change dated 2027-01-19

priority_boarding.delta_one_basic_business: Zone 1 boarding is included even on the Basic Business fare.

delta.rule: Main Cabin and above (non-Basic) fares originating in the US have no change fee. 'Extra' fares are fully refundable to the original form of payment. Basic fares change or cancel for a fee; Main Basic retains a $99 change fee, and reporting says the unbundled premium Basic tiers carry fees up to $500.
delta.verification: secondary (the fee amounts come from trade press; Delta's change-cancel page was not fetched)

united.rule: Only the Flexible tier of Polaris and Premium Plus is refundable; Standard allows changes but is nonrefundable; Base allows neither.

american.note: American's fare-rule pages returned 403. Not confirmed.

us_law_all_cabins.rule: Under DOT's 2024 refund rule, airlines must refund automatically, in the original form of payment, when they cancel or significantly change a flight and the passenger does not travel, and must refund the checked-bag fee when a bag is not delivered within 12 hours of a domestic flight arriving at the gate (15 to 30 hours for international, depending on flight length).
us_law_all_cabins.period: Final rule April 2024; reinforced by the FAA Reauthorization Act of 16 May 2024

re_entrainment_rate_hours_per_day.quote: Westward travel: 1.5 hrs/day; eastward travel: 1 hr/day
re_entrainment_rate_hours_per_day.reason: The intrinsic human circadian period is slightly longer than 24 hours, so delaying the clock (westward) is easier than advancing it (eastward).
re_entrainment_rate_hours_per_day.citation: Riedy SM, Williams SG. Jet Lag Disorder. CDC Yellow Book: Health Information for International Travel, 2026 edition.

peer_reviewed_corroboration.citation: Eastman CI, Burgess HJ. How to travel the world without jet lag. Sleep Medicine Clinics 2009;4(2):241-255. PMID 20204161
peer_reviewed_corroboration.finding: Circadian phase delayed about 1.5 h/day after westward flights and advanced about 1 h/day after eastward flights.
peer_reviewed_corroboration.verification: secondary (the figure is as cited by a 2024 aircrew resynchronisation paper; the Eastman and Burgess full text could not be retrieved)

direction_asymmetry_over_5_zones.finding: After crossing more than five time zones, the average rate of westward adaptation is about 50% higher than eastward (Aschoff, 1995).

threshold_time_zones.clinical_quote: Insomnia or excessive daytime sleepiness, accompanied by a reduction of total sleep time, associated with trans-meridian travel across at least two time zones.
threshold_time_zones.clinical_basis: ICSD-3 criterion A as given in the CDC Yellow Book 2026
threshold_time_zones.symptom_onset: Impairment of daytime function, general malaise or somatic symptoms within 1 to 2 days after travel (ICSD-3 criterion B).
threshold_time_zones.review_quote: jet lag refers to a collection of symptoms that occur in the days after flight across three or more time zones
threshold_time_zones.review_citation: Roach GD, Sargent C. Interventions to Minimize Jet Lag After Westward and Eastward Flight. Frontiers in Physiology 2019;10:927. PMID 31417411
threshold_time_zones.verification: fetched (CDC); fetched via Europe PMC full text (Roach and Sargent)
threshold_time_zones.note: The two sources differ: 2 zones is the diagnostic floor for jet lag disorder, 3 zones is a common working definition. Neither publishes a hard cut-off below which effects are zero.

effects.symptoms: Sleep disturbances, cognitive impairment, daytime sleepiness, general malaise, gastrointestinal disturbances, and/or other symptoms.

prevalence_business_travellers.quote: 68% of international business travelers experienced negative symptoms on a regular basis
prevalence_business_travellers.period: Survey cited in CDC Yellow Book 2026

waterhouse_lancet_2007.citation: Waterhouse J, Reilly T, Atkinson G, Edwards B. Jet lag: trends and coping strategies. Lancet 2007;369(9567):1117-1129. PMID 17398311
waterhouse_lancet_2007.finding: Abstract emphasises sleep loss and decreased performance, caused mainly by the body clock being mistimed for the new time zone; advice differs by direction of flight. The abstract gives no numeric rate.

sack_nejm_2010.citation: Sack RL. Clinical practice. Jet lag. N Engl J Med 2010;362(5):440-447. doi:10.1056/NEJMcp0909838. PMID 20130253
sack_nejm_2010.note: Paywalled; no abstract text retrievable. Cited for completeness only; no figures are taken from it.

performance_quantified.citation: Song A, Severini T, Allada R. How jet lag impairs Major League Baseball performance. PNAS 2017;114(6):1407-1412. PMID 28115724
performance_quantified.finding: Jet-lag effects appeared largely after eastward travel with very limited effects after westward travel. Jet lag impaired home-team offence (e.g. slugging percentage) and both teams' defence, with most of the effect explained by home runs allowed.

performance_quantified.citation: Leota J, Hoffman D, Czeisler MÉ, Mascaro L, Drummond SPA, Anderson C, Rajaratnam SMW, Facer-Childs ER. Eastward Jet Lag is Associated with Impaired Performance and Game Outcome in the National Basketball Association. Frontiers in Physiology 2022.
performance_quantified.finding: Eastward, not westward, jet lag was associated with lower winning percentage (-6.03 points, p = 0.051), points differential (-1.29 points, p = 0.015) and rebound differential (-1.29 rebounds, p < 0.0001).

fhwa_urban_congestion_report.definition: Travel Time Index = weekday peak-period travel time divided by free-flow travel time (1.28 means peak trips take 28% longer). Planning Time Index is the 95th-percentile equivalent.
fhwa_urban_congestion_report.note: FHWA publishes ratios, not mph. A travel-time model would multiply a free-flow time by the TTI in peak periods.

uncertain.item: Average fare or fare per mile by cabin from BTS DB1B
uncertain.reason: No BTS table or peer-reviewed paper was found that publishes averages by DB1B fare class (C/D/F/G against X/Y). The GMU DB1B primer reports that DOT itself cautions that FareClass is coded inconsistently across carriers. A ratio could be computed from the raw DB1B coupon files, but it would be SLATE's own analysis, not a published figure.

uncertain.item: US domestic first/business to coach fare ratio
uncertain.reason: Not published by DOT or BTS. The only published multiple is IATA's global, mostly international ~5x (premium against economy, 2023-24), which blends long-haul business with short-haul first.

uncertain.item: Premium economy markup over economy (percent)
uncertain.reason: No primary source publishes it. Consumer sites say 50-100% (Simple Flying, Going, Skyscanner): unsourced estimates, not recorded as figures. The academic evidence is a production-cost multiple (1.6x, Hugon-Duprat and O'Connell 2015) and survey willingness to pay (Kuo and Jou 2017), neither of which is a fare markup.

uncertain.item: Hugon-Duprat and O'Connell (2015) '2.3 times' revenue figure
uncertain.reason: The RePEc summary says premium economy seats 'generate 2.3 times higher revenues' but does not say whether that is relative to economy revenue or to the seat's own production cost; a search excerpt read it as relative to cost. Full text is paywalled.

uncertain.item: American Airlines free checked-bag count and refund rules by premium cabin
uncertain.reason: aa.com returned 403. American's April 2026 release confirms that premium cabins get complimentary bags but gives no count.

uncertain.item: Delta and United free-bag counts on operator pages
uncertain.reason: Delta's own pages confirm complimentary bags for premium cabins and the 70 lb limit for Delta One and First, but the count (2) is from third-party guides. United's tiers (1 bag Base, 2 bags Standard or Flexible) come from AFAR; united.com timed out.

uncertain.item: United 2026 economy bag fees
uncertain.reason: united.com timed out; figures from NerdWallet and CNBC.

uncertain.item: Delta Basic premium change and cancel fees (up to $500)
uncertain.reason: Trade-press figure; Delta's change-cancel page was not fetched.

uncertain.item: Eastman and Burgess (2009) 1.5 h/day west, 1 h/day east; Aschoff (1995) 50% faster west
uncertain.reason: Full texts not retrieved; figures as cited by a 2024 aircrew paper. The same 1.5 and 1.0 h/day figures are confirmed directly in the CDC Yellow Book 2026 (primary).

uncertain.item: Sack, NEJM 2010
uncertain.reason: Paywalled and no abstract available through Europe PMC.

uncertain.item: Quantified cognitive or alertness deficit per time zone in the general population
uncertain.reason: No peer-reviewed source found that gives a per-zone or per-day cognitive decrement for ordinary travellers. The quantified effects found are from athletes (MLB, NBA) and show an eastward-only effect.

uncertain.item: AAA medium-sedan fuel and maintenance cents per mile
uncertain.reason: The AAA fact sheet gives fuel (17.3 cents) and maintenance, repair and tires (11.7 cents) only as all-vehicle averages. Medium sedan is given only as a total (70.37 cents/mile in 2026). The per-model breakdown is behind AAA's 'click here' link, which was not retrieved. Note: some search snippets attribute 66.11 cents to the 2025 medium sedan; that is the 2025 subcompact SUV. The 2025 medium sedan was 66.37 cents.

uncertain.reason: flylax.com returned 403. Figures come from search-index excerpts of LAX's own pages. An older excerpt gave Economy Lot E as $12/day, which appears stale.

uncertain.reason: The Massport page fetched gave only Terminal B ($46) and Economy ($37). Third-party sites say Central is also $46, but that is not confirmed from Massport.

uncertain.reason: The latest Port Authority schedules found are the January 2025 editions, with rates effective 8 July 2024. JFK's is the January 2026 edition. A 2026 LGA or EWR revision may exist but was not found.

uncertain.reason: FHWA publishes travel-time indices, not speeds, in the Urban Congestion Report. INRIX's downtown speeds are in its interactive city pages, which were not retrievable. No federal national average mph was found.
